what_it_is.prose: The HAL HS-748, universally known in Indian service as the 'Avro', is a British Hawker Siddeley twin-turboprop medium transport that HAL licence-built in India. The first Indian-assembled HAL-748 flew on 1 November 1961, and by the end of production HAL had completed 89 Indian-built aircraft — 72 for the Indian Air Force and 17 for the national carrier Indian Airlines. Powered by two imported Rolls-Royce Dart turboprops, the Avro became a workhorse of Indian military and civil aviation for decades. It is now the oldest aircraft type in IAF service and has been progressively relegated from primary transport to communication and navigation/transport-training duties. The fleet is being phased out and replaced by the Airbus C-295: India ordered 56 C-295 aircraft (about $2.4 billion), of which 16 are supplied in flyaway condition from Airbus in Spain and the remaining 40 are being manufactured in India by Tata Advanced Systems Limited (TASL) at Vadodara, Gujarat — the first C-295s entering IAF service from 2023. The Avro-to-C-295 transition is symbolically significant because both the outgoing and incoming fleets are Indian-built, marking continuity in HAL/TASL transport-aircraft manufacture. The Atlas records the HS-748 as a legacy licence-built platform of genuine historical India relevance, now at the end of its service life.

deployments_procurement.summary: The HS-748 was licence-built by HAL, with 89 aircraft produced (72 IAF, 17 Indian Airlines) from the early 1960s. It is India's oldest aircraft type still flying, now in a communication/training role, and is being replaced by the Airbus C-295 (56 aircraft; 16 from Spain, 40 built by TASL at Vadodara), which began entering IAF service in 2023.

import_dependencies.summary: Although licence-built by HAL, the HS-748 is a British design powered by imported Rolls-Royce Dart turboprops, with legacy avionics of foreign origin. As a retiring type, its principal current constraint is spares/obsolescence rather than new-build supply. Its C-295 replacement shifts a substantial share of production to India (TASL Vadodara), though the C-295's Pratt & Whitney Canada engines remain imported.
